name: Zoe Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. This is confidential. Tell me about a normal morning at Market Square.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The coffee usually goes cold while I match online sales to bank deposits. I'm Zoe Schmidt, forty-three, and I prepare accounts and tax returns for small internet sellers. I earned a bachelor's in accounting after years running the books for an arts program, but tax exceptions still send me to my supervisor, so I'm a junior here. I use AI every day to draft questions, then check the source statement before sending them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Which part do you enjoy, and what gets difficult?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when a seller finally sees why sales are not the same as cash in the bank. I still misread refunds and need help with unusual tax treatment. My partner Kit is a self-employed electrician, our children are ten and thirteen, and we have a mortgage. My pay is typical for this job, our five-month reserve covers his slow periods, and there are some similar accounting firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be a little disappointed after all the testing, but a reliable small gain is still useful. I use AI every day to draft questions about online sales, then check the answers against the seller's statements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell clients that faster sorting does not mean a return should go out unchecked. I'd tell the team to keep the parts that save time and put the saved hour into learning, not a higher daily file target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job and our mortgage seem manageable in this picture. I'm forty-three, a junior at Market Square Tax after a late accounting degree, and still learning the odd tax rules. Kit's electrical jobs vary by season, but my pay is normal and we have five months of expenses saved, with some firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tested daily drafts and the supervisor's final review. I'd leave the five-month reserve untouched and put another fifty a month into it when Kit's booked jobs actually pay. In the first year of a plateau, I'd ask for a paid half day to work through the sales-tax mistakes I logged in October.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the uneven bills, though not afraid of losing this job. Some months Kit's invoices land late and the mortgage does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which draft mistake taught you something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A ceramics seller's platform called a refund a sale, and the draft copied the mistake. I caught it against the bank statement before the return was signed. I keep a note of that error because it tells me what to ask next time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would the extra fifty enter savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd only add fifty after Kit's invoices clear, not when a client says payment is coming. Last year two of his electrical jobs slipped into the next month. Our reserve covers late electrical invoices, but I count cash only when it clears.

say: I would keep **human review** on faster online sales returns before anything goes to a client.
I would use saved time for **paid learning**.
think: My **five-month reserve** protects ordinary income gaps when electrical invoices are paid late.
Kit’s **late invoices** still make the mortgage date uncomfortable.
do: Keep **daily checked drafts** and supervisor sign-off.
Save **fifty extra** only when Kit’s invoices clear.
Request a **paid half day** on logged sales-tax errors.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about uneven cash despite stable work.
S0.quote: Our reserve covers late electrical invoices, but I count cash only when it clears.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI habit** is balanced by bank-statement checks after a copied refund error.
A **five-month cushion** covers timing gaps, though partner invoices make her uneasy.

steps.text: Keep daily AI draft checks and supervisor sign-off
Save fifty extra monthly only after partner invoices clear
Study logged sales-tax errors if paid half day approved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This sounds like what our online-seller desk is walking toward. The software already writes client questions and checks sales feeds; fewer juniors might be needed once it books everything too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd ask for the pilot results to show mistakes, hours and staffing. I'd tell friends that a fair rollout should pay for new skills and keep people in the room with clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become the junior who manages the system, but that is not a guaranteed full week. My own paid hours may shrink if the partners combine two small teams. Five months saved helps, yet Kit's uneven electrical income cannot cover our mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose a thirty-file pilot on online sellers and build an error sheet the whole team can check. I'd teach two colleagues the review panel during paid time if the partner approves it. If the firm cuts my hours anyway, I'd apply for the funded credit-union operations vacancy only if its published wage covers the mortgage and the start date is fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the work I enjoy could become an excuse to reduce my rota. I would still rather see the results myself than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at home if hours fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter Bea has a school concert in April, and I would not cut the tickets on a rumour. If my hours actually fall, we'd first stop the weekend takeaways. I would not budget more electrical shifts until customers confirm them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should see the error sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The partners should see the original receipts beside every wrong flag. I'd ask the staff association to put paid review time into the pilot agreement. If they refuse, we can still document what the machine gets wrong without promising everybody a new role.

say: I would publish **mistakes, hours and staffing** together before the partners change our paid rota.
I would seek **paid review time** for colleagues.
think: My **paid week** could shrink when the partners combine two small teams.
Kit’s **uneven invoices** cannot replace a lost accounting day.
do: Pilot **thirty seller files** and log wrong flags.
Teach **two colleagues** the review panel only if paid time is approved.
Apply for **funded credit-union work** if hours fall and pay covers mortgage.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own rota.
S1.quote: I would not budget more electrical shifts until customers confirm them.
fieldNote: The **thirty-file pilot** uses her daily tool knowledge to test an exposed desk task.
Her **credit-union application** requires funded work, a published mortgage-covering wage and a fixed start date.

steps.text: Pilot AI review on thirty seller files and log wrong flags
Teach two colleagues review panel if paid time approved
Ask staff association for paid review time in pilot agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 means the software could do the whole online-seller desk before my younger child leaves primary school. I use the tools gladly now, but I do not mistake that for ownership of the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask employers to publish staffing dates and support staff who lose jobs. I'd also argue for public wage support so families do not have to burn through savings while whole occupations shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior accounting role to go in the first year after full AGI arrives in 2028. It is thinking work on a screen, so robots around 2031 don't give my tax job extra time. Our five-month reserve is real, but Kit's electrical jobs aren't always booked ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the family holiday this month, stop adding to its account and keep that hundred in cash for bills. I'd apply for the open library finance vacancy if it is funded and pays enough for our mortgage, while knowing it is also desk work. In the first year after 2028, if the firm cuts me, I'd claim wage support and ask the lender for temporary terms before the reserve is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, despite having more cash than we did a few years ago. A five-month reserve runs down quickly when two incomes wobble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your partner simply work more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kit which jobs are already signed and which are only enquiries. I would not ask him to promise six days a week when customers have not booked them. We'd tell the children the holiday can wait, then keep school costs in the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the library move real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The library job needs a published salary and start date; I would not resign on a rumour. I'd put the hundred from the holiday account into the bill account only once. If the vacancy closes, I stay employed and keep looking.

say: I would seek **published staffing dates** and help for anyone losing accounting hours.
I would ask for **wage support** during displacement.
think: My **screen job** could end soon after 2028.
Five months saved may shrink fast with **unbooked electrical work**.
do: Cancel the **family holiday** and hold its one-time hundred for bills.
Apply for **funded library work** with mortgage-covering pay and confirmed start; if closed, keep current pay while searching.
Claim **wage support** and ask lender for temporary terms after a cut.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about both incomes wobbling.
S2.quote: A five-month reserve runs down quickly when two incomes wobble.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches her accounting role in 2028, before robots enter hands-on work.
The **holiday transfer** becomes cash for bills, without assuming unconfirmed electrical work or a library vacancy.

steps.text: Cancel family holiday and hold one-time hundred for bills
Apply for funded library work only with mortgage-covering pay and confirmed start date
Keep current pay while searching if library vacancy closes
Claim wage support after 2028 dismissal and request lender terms before cash runs out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me test a different service with real people, not just take another online course. Standard returns could still be cheap by 2031, which is the deadline for my screen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to share the gains by paying for training and client time. I'd ask our staff association to bargain for actual vacancies or paid transitions rather than a promise of future roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could help self-employed workers plan for uneven months, which I understand from our home. AI might draft the budget, but people may still want a person to ask questions. Robots around 2034 do not change the 2031 date for my tax desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol in the three-hundred cash-flow coaching course if Market Square pays the fee and gives paid study time. I'd run six supervised client sessions during normal hours if the partner approves them and clients agree. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my tax post ends, I'd apply for a funded coaching vacancy only if its salary covers the mortgage. If the firm refuses paid study or the fee, I'd keep my return wage and attend free credit-union workshops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with room to check whether anyone values those sessions. My own family has five months saved, so I won't spend that reserve on a course the firm could fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would six clients tell you if there is demand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six people would be enough to learn what questions come up twice. I'd record whether they return, not just whether they thank me. If no client books a second cash-flow session, the service is not ready to carry a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm refuses course funding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fee and study hours both need approval in writing. If either is refused, I'd use free credit-union workshops and keep working the returns. I would not call a free workshop the same as supervised client practice.

say: I would seek **paid training** and client time.
I would ask for **real vacancies** through the staff association.
think: My **tax desk** is exposed in 2031 even though I use AI every day.
Six **client sessions** could test demand for cash-flow coaching.
do: Enrol in **coaching study** if firm funds fee and time; otherwise keep return pay and use free workshops.
Run **six supervised sessions** if partner and clients agree.
Apply after **2031 tax job loss** for funded coaching work only if pay covers mortgage.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but able to test demand.
S3.quote: If no client books a second cash-flow session, the service is not ready to carry a wage.
fieldNote: **Written funding** and paid time protect her household reserve while she tests a new service.

steps.text: Enrol in coaching course if firm funds fee and paid study
Run six supervised sessions during paid hours if partner and clients agree
Apply for funded coaching vacancy after 2031 tax job loss if salary covers mortgage
Attend free credit-union workshops and keep return pay if funded study refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would give me time to build relationships beyond a tax return. I'd be fifty-three in 2036, with children grown and perhaps a smaller mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say productivity gains should pay for shorter weeks and training places, not just larger partner drawings. I'd support a public fund when small firms cannot finance a career change themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Routine returns will still shrink when thinking AI reaches full strength in 2036. A cash-flow clinic might become paid work by then, but only if enough clients book it. Robots around 2039 do not lengthen my present desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run one paid Saturday clinic at the community centre this year if four self-employed clients book and cover the room fee. I'd keep the hundred monthly household savings transfer when Kit's invoices clear, rather than spend the reserve on advertising. In the first year after AGI in 2036, if my tax role ends, I'd expand the clinic only if six months of signed bookings cover our mortgage; otherwise I'd apply for a funded advice vacancy that pays the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but a decade lets me stop experiments that do not pay. A business idea is not a wage just because my friends like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you commit to the first clinic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book the community room for one Saturday, not a whole season. If four clients don't pay ahead, I'd cancel without risking the mortgage account. The reserve belongs to the family before it belongs to a new service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as enough to expand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need six months of signed bookings and invoices paid, not a list of interested people. If the clinic cannot clear that line, I'd keep my job while possible and apply only for funded advice posts with a salary that covers our mortgage. I will not use the children's savings for a trial.

say: I would seek **shorter weeks** and paid learning while the firm still earns from returns.
I would back a **public fund** for small-firm workers.
think: My **tax desk** still shrinks by 2036, even if I build another service.
A **paid clinic** needs booked clients and mortgage-covering revenue.
do: Run one **paid Saturday clinic** only if four clients prepay room fee; keep tax work meanwhile.
Save **one hundred monthly** after Kit’s invoices clear; keep tax pay if the clinic fails.
After **2036 tax job loss**, expand only with six mortgage months signed and paid; otherwise seek funded mortgage-covering advice work.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but able to stop weak experiments.
S4.quote: A business idea is not a wage just because my friends like it.
fieldNote: A **single-room booking** limits the cost of her side experiment while she tests whether clients actually pay.
The **2036 expansion** requires six months of mortgage-covering signed bookings and paid invoices.

steps.text: Run one Saturday clinic if four clients prepay room fee while keeping tax job
Save one hundred monthly only after partner invoices clear
Expand after 2036 job loss only with six months mortgage-covering signed bookings and paid invoices
Apply for funded advice post after 2036 job loss if clinic fails and wage covers mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My screen role could end before a client clinic has repeat bookings, while Kit's electrical work may not be booked every week. Wage support, published staffing plans, paid supervised training and funded vacancies would help. I can test a service, but I cannot count a compliment as a paid invoice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how families count uncertain work. I know Kit's enquiries are not shifts until the customer signs. A new advice service needs the same honesty; a booking has to pay the mortgage before I call it a livelihood.

headlineQuote: I can test a service, but I cannot count a compliment as a paid invoice.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Zoe is a junior tax accountant serving online sellers after later accounting study.
Her **bachelor’s** and daily AI use coexist with supervisor checks on unfamiliar tax rules.
A **mortgage**, two schoolchildren and variable electrical income sit beside five months saved.
Some **nearby firms** offer options, though she tests funded training and client demand first.
She treats **paid invoices** and confirmed jobs as evidence before expanding any advice clinic.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her screen role before a clinic has repeat paying clients.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **wage support**, public staffing plans, paid supervised training and funded vacancies.
